interest: Shows 1946 U.S. officials weighing wheat allocations between starving occupied Japan and liberated Europe.
overview: Two February-March 1946 State memos debate diverting wheat from France, Italy, and occupied Germany to meet MacArthur's request for 1.5 million tons to avert Japanese starvation, ultimately recommending increased March-April shipments to sustain a 900-calorie daily ration.

people.name: William L. Clayton
people.role: Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs

people.name: James A. Stillwell
people.role: Adviser on Supplies and Resources, International Resources Division

people.name: Douglas MacArthur
people.role: General of the Army / Supreme Commander for the Allied Powers

subfiles.about: Memorandum arguing against reducing European wheat allocations to fulfill the U.S. Army's wheat request for Japan.
subfiles.from: H. Freeman Matthews (Office of European Affairs)
subfiles.summary: Matthews warns that meeting the Army's 1,500,000-ton wheat request for Japan would force cuts to Europe, risking unrest in France, Italy, and Germany's western zones, with little real benefit to starving Japan; he urges prioritizing Europe.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from H. Freeman Matthews to William L. Clayton on Wheat Allocations for Europe and Japan
subfiles.to: William L. Clayton (Assistant Secretary of State for Economic Affairs)

subfiles.about: Memorandum recommending an immediate increase in wheat allocations to Japan for March and April 1946 to prevent mass starvation.
subfiles.summary: Stillwell urges committing 150,000 tons of wheat for Japan in March and 200,000 in April to avert MacArthur-reported famine, sustaining a 900-calorie diet, backed by Army Transportation Corps shipping capacity despite cautious Agriculture Department estimates.
subfiles.title: Memorandum from James A. Stillwell to Dean Acheson on Allocation of Wheat to Japan for March and April
